11	The constraint framework requires no architectural modification: the grammar layer compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned entity type constraints via the same stateful registry mechanism.
12	The violation taxonomy extends naturally: Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR), Entity Type (ET), and Cross-Field (CF).

55	\paragraph{Results.}
56	Unconstrained generation produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV exceeding 85\% combined; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), and all models yield entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot identify well-formed mentions in off-schema output.
57	Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all three models ($\to$\,0\%), validating tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
58	Grammar-only ablation isolates each layer: grammar eliminates EV ($\to$\,0\%) but leaves RoV at 64--77\% because the CFG cannot constrain 80 argument roles conditioned on event context; AC rises from near-zero to 8--14\%, replicating the latent-violation surfacing pattern from DocRED (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}).

% v3 final data confirmed by Director 2026-05-18.

\subsection{Cross-Task Validation: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
The constraint framework requires no architectural modification: the grammar layer compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned entity type constraints via the same stateful registry mechanism.
The violation taxonomy extends naturally: Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR), Entity Type (ET), and Cross-Field (CF).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: WikiEvents three-model comparison (v3 final)
%  exp_ids: ee_{qwen,llama,mistral}_wikievents_{unconstrained,grammar_only,constrained_v3}
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.8pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Mode}
  & EV\,$\downarrow$ & RoV\,$\downarrow$ & AC & CF
  & Trig.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Unconstr.\ & 24.0 & 74.9 & 0.3 & 0 & 11.8 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 76.1 & 8.2 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 2.1 & 21.1 & 13.4 & 14.1 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Llama\\3.1-8B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 10.5 & 88.8 & 0.1 & 0 & 5.7 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 77.0 & 8.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 3.8 & 17.2 & 7.5 & 17.6 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Mistral\\7B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 37.3 & 63.9 & 0 & 0 & 2.4 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 64.0 & 13.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 1.3 & 14.9 & 3.9 & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{WikiEvents EE results (246 documents, zero-shot).
Violation rates over parsed documents.
---: not applicable (grammar-only has no semantic-layer metrics).
F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:wikievents}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained generation produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV exceeding 85\% combined; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), and all models yield entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot identify well-formed mentions in off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all three models ($\to$\,0\%), validating tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
Grammar-only ablation isolates each layer: grammar eliminates EV ($\to$\,0\%) but leaves RoV at 64--77\% because the CFG cannot constrain 80 argument roles conditioned on event context; AC rises from near-zero to 8--14\%, replicating the latent-violation surfacing pattern from DocRED (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}).
Full S1 then drives RoV to 0\%, confirming layer complementarity.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to confusion between semantically similar entity types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN) where grammar-first fallback permits the incorrect type; CF rises to 15--21\%, consistent with the per-slot enforcement trade-off in RE.

Post-hoc filtering is impractical for EE: it retains only 23/5{,}467 arguments for Qwen (99.6\% discarded), 3/5{,}053 for Llama, and 0/6{,}034 for Mistral, because unconstrained models generate generic role names rather than ontology-specific ones.
Unlike RE, where constraints are F1-neutral, EE shows measurable gains: entity F1 rises from 0\% to 11.7--17.6\% and trigger F1 increases by $+$1.5--1.8\,pp, because grammar enforcement produces schema-valid JSON that the parser can process.

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC,
evaluating each constraint layer independently and in combination.
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 551 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters;
only the active constraint layers differ.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
DR: domain/range violation rate;
RV: relation vocabulary violation rate;
ET: entity type violation rate;
CF: cross-field consistency violation rate.
$\Delta$DR: relative DR reduction vs.\ the unconstrained baseline.
$\downarrow$\,/\,$\uparrow$: lower\,/\,higher is better.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded; see text).
F1 scores are multiplied by 100.
Statistical significance assessed via bootstrap resampling (10{,}000 iterations).}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
At the per-relation level, violations drop from 42.42\% to 2.82\% on
\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004
The residual ET under semantic-only arises because the semantic mask constrains type tokens to relation-specific valid sets but cannot enforce vocabulary membership; occasionally the mask excludes the model's preferred valid-vocabulary type, forcing an OOV alternative.
Under full mode, the grammar layer's intersection prevents this, confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV relation types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% relative reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} presents the composability matrix on SciERC for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (zero-shot vs.\ LoRA fine-tuned $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ full S1), testing whether OntoCoDec composes with task-specific fine-tuning across model families.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
The four-way ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) shows grammar is a no-op post-fine-tuning; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\%.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned) for Qwen, tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) offers an orthogonal path: on SciERC, it eliminates residual DR entirely and reduces CF from 9.90\% to 0.53\% for Qwen, and from 6.56\% to 0.93\% for Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll rrrr r@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Mode}
  & \textbf{DR\,$\downarrow$} & \textbf{CF}
  & \textbf{R-F1\,$\uparrow$} & \textbf{E-F1\,$\uparrow$}
  & \textbf{$\Delta$DR} \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{Qwen3-8B}

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Composability matrix on SciERC (551 documents):
zero-shot vs.\ LoRA fine-tuned $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ full S1
for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.

% exp_ids: ee_qwen_wikievents_unconstrained, ee_llama_wikievents_unconstrained,

% v3 final data confirmed by Director 2026-05-18.

\subsection{Cross-Task Validation: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
The constraint framework requires no architectural modification: the grammar layer compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned entity type constraints via the same stateful registry mechanism.
The violation taxonomy extends naturally: Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR), Entity Type (ET), and Cross-Field (CF).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: WikiEvents three-model comparison (v3 final)
%  exp_ids: ee_{qwen,llama,mistral}_wikievents_{unconstrained,grammar_only,constrained_v3}
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.8pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Mode}
  & EV\,$\downarrow$ & RoV\,$\downarrow$ & AC & CF
  & Trig.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Unconstr.\ & 24.0 & 74.9 & 0.3 & 0 & 11.8 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 76.1 & 8.2 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 2.1 & 21.1 & 13.4 & 14.1 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Llama\\3.1-8B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 10.5 & 88.8 & 0.1 & 0 & 5.7 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 77.0 & 8.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 3.8 & 17.2 & 7.5 & 17.6 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Mistral\\7B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 37.3 & 63.9 & 0 & 0 & 2.4 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 64.0 & 13.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 1.3 & 14.9 & 3.9 & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{WikiEvents EE results (246 documents, zero-shot).
Violation rates over parsed documents.
---: not applicable (grammar-only has no semantic-layer metrics).
F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:wikievents}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained generation produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV exceeding 85\% combined; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), and all models yield entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot identify well-formed mentions in off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all three models ($\to$\,0\%), validating tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
Grammar-only ablation isolates each layer: grammar eliminates EV ($\to$\,0\%) but leaves RoV at 64--77\% because the CFG cannot constrain 80 argument roles conditioned on event context; AC rises from near-zero to 8--14\%, replicating the latent-violation surfacing pattern from DocRED (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}).
Full S1 then drives RoV to 0\%, confirming layer complementarity.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to confusion between semantically similar entity types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN) where grammar-first fallback permits the incorrect type; CF rises to 15--21\%, consistent with the per-slot enforcement trade-off in RE.

Post-hoc filtering is impractical for EE: it retains only 23/5{,}467 arguments for Qwen (99.6\% discarded), 3/5{,}053 for Llama, and 0/6{,}034 for Mistral, because unconstrained models generate generic role names rather than ontology-specific ones.
Unlike RE, where constraints are F1-neutral, EE shows measurable gains: entity F1 rises from 0\% to 11.7--17.6\% and trigger F1 increases by $+$1.5--1.8\,pp, because grammar enforcement produces schema-valid JSON that the parser can process.

% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments

% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC,
evaluating each constraint layer independently and in combination.
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 551 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters;
only the active constraint layers differ.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}

\toprule

  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF

\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar

  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}

  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\

\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
The four-way ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) shows grammar is a no-op post-fine-tuning; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\%.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned) for Qwen, tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) offers an orthogonal path: on SciERC, it eliminates residual DR entirely and reduces CF from 9.90\% to 0.53\% for Qwen, and from 6.56\% to 0.93\% for Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).

F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
The four-way ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) shows grammar is a no-op post-fine-tuning; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\%.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned) for Qwen, tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) offers an orthogonal path: on SciERC, it eliminates residual DR entirely and reduces CF from 9.90\% to 0.53\% for Qwen, and from 6.56\% to 0.93\% for Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
Post-fine-tuning, grammar is a no-op; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\% (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}).
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates residual DR and reduces CF to $<$1\% for both Qwen and Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll rrrr r@{}}
\toprule

\midrule

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation} presents the four-way ablation on DocRED, a document-level RE benchmark with 96 Wikidata relation types (14$\times$ the ontology size of SciERC).

  & 1.05
  & 7.70  & 57.81 \\

\label{tab:docred-ablation}
\end{table}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%; residual traces to tokenization edge cases where multi-token relation names span grammar-state boundaries).
Relation F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81], $p < 0.001$), attributable to grammar-layer elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions counted as false positives.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), lower than SciERC's 9.90\%, consistent with the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off analyzed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR to 26.17\% ($+$42\%): the baseline's 29.66\% OOV triples cannot be evaluated for DR; grammar enforcement assigns valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated types frequently violate, \emph{revealing} latent incompatibilities that motivate the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency and tightness ceiling.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by 25\% but cannot eliminate RV (29.87\%) or prevent ET increases (2.48\%\,$\to$\,4.22\%), replicating SciERC's enabling dependency.
Residual DR (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC's (0.93\%) due to higher constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$ vs.\ 0.333), with fallback rate (10.2\%) closely tracking residual DR (Appendix~\ref{app:fallback-coverage}).

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: for calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%; including Mistral (whose high baseline ET shifts the regime), the full range across all three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; quantitative analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
The sequential masking strategy ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are overwhelmingly non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) \wedge \tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r)$) would admit 33.3\% (SciERC) and 36.8\% (DocRED) spurious type pairs. On SciERC, 100\% of residual DR violations under full S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.
OntoCoDec's sequential approach achieves exact pair-based enforcement without explicit enumeration of $\sigma(r)$ at each step, exploiting the autoregressive left-to-right generation order.

\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
We classify constraints by when sufficient information becomes available: \emph{local} (current token only, e.g., vocabulary membership; grammar layer), \emph{prefix-decidable} (decoded prefix, e.g., domain/range; semantic layer), and \emph{non-local} (forward coreference; outside single-pass decoding, partially addressed by S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).

CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: for calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%; including Mistral (whose high baseline ET shifts the regime), the full range across all three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; quantitative analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
We classify constraints by when sufficient information becomes available: \emph{local} (current token only, e.g., vocabulary membership; grammar layer), \emph{prefix-decidable} (decoded prefix, e.g., domain/range; semantic layer), and \emph{non-local} (forward coreference; outside single-pass decoding, partially addressed by S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints that provide formal guarantees during autoregressive generation:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar context-free grammar) guaranteeing JSON structural validity and entity/relation vocabulary membership (virtually eliminating entity type and relation vocabulary violations); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} guaranteeing per-triple domain/range type compliance via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
The two layers compose via bitwise AND on logit masks, with the grammar layer as an enabling prerequisite.
%
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations: 15.37\% on SciERC (7 relations) and 18.46\% on DocRED (96 relations), comparable rates governed by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology scale.
\textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR by 42--99\% across three model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) with no significant F1 cost.
For the primary model (Qwen3-8B): SciERC $+$0.13\,pp ($p{=}0.58$), DocRED $+$0.50\,pp ($p{<}0.001$); other models show comparable or larger gains (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1, mistral_docred
For calibrated models, residual DR correlates with the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate, suggesting that constraint effectiveness is predictable from schema and model characteristics.
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, DR reaches $\leq$\,0.09\% (SciERC) and 0.20\% (DocRED) with relation F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming near-lossless composability.
With beam search ($k{=}4$), the full stack (LoRA + OntoCoDec + beam) achieves zero constraint violations across all four categories while preserving extraction quality (relation F1 change ${<}$0.5\,pp).
The framework generalizes to event extraction (WikiEvents: 56 event types, 80 roles) without architectural modification and eliminates event-vocabulary and role-vocabulary violations ($\to$ 0\%); where unconstrained outputs are severely off-schema, format compliance additionally enables entity extraction (Entity F1: 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly deployed for zero-shot information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
In a systematic study, we find violations are pervasive: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred}, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.
Relations with tight constraints exhibit far higher rates (\textsc{Compare}: 42.4\%) than loosely constrained ones (\textsc{Used-for}: 0.8\%).

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, enabling the semantic layer to look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
On SciERC, OntoCoDec reduces DR violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while remaining F1-neutral ($+$0.13\,pp).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), showing that violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and that prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Empirical validation on 3 models $\times$ 3 datasets (2 RE + 1 EE): DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC and $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED, with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); cross-task generalization to event extraction on WikiEvents (vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\%; format compliance enables entity extraction, Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%); composability with fine-tuning (DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost); and characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%).
    Composability with LoRA fine-tuning is near-lossless: the full stack (fine-tuning + constrained decoding + beam search) eliminates all four violation types while preserving R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
\end{enumerate}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_grammar_only,
%          phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation} presents the four-way ablation on DocRED (96 Wikidata relation types, 14$\times$ SciERC; Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 998 documents).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: DocRED four-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 18.46 & ---
  & 29.66 & 2.48
  & 0.10
  & 7.74  & 58.15 \\
Grammar
  & 26.17 & $\uparrow$42\%
  & \textbf{0.03} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.07
  & \textbf{8.31}  & \textbf{59.38} \\
Semantic
  & 13.84 & $\downarrow$25\%
  & 29.87 & 4.22
  & 1.05
  & 7.70  & 57.81 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{10.21} & $\downarrow$\textbf{45\%}
  & \textbf{0.03} & \textbf{0}
  & 2.57
  & 8.23  & 59.37 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Four-way ablation on DocRED (998 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap significance: R-F1 $+$0.50\,pp ($p < 0.001$).}
\label{tab:docred-ablation}
\end{table}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET ($\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
R-F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; $p < 0.001$), attributable to elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), consistent with the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR to 26.17\% ($+$42\%): the baseline's 29.66\% OOV triples cannot be evaluated for DR; grammar enforcement assigns valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated types frequently violate, \emph{revealing} latent incompatibilities that motivate the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency and tightness ceiling.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by 25\% but cannot eliminate RV (29.87\%) or prevent ET increases (2.48\%\,$\to$\,4.22\%), replicating SciERC's enabling dependency.
Residual DR (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC's (0.93\%) due to higher constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$ vs.\ 0.333), with fallback rate (10.2\%) closely tracking residual DR (Appendix~\ref{app:fallback-coverage}).
